# Validity, fairness and governance of AI {#ai-validity}

<div class="goals">
**Learning goals.** After this chapter you can

* place an AI component in the **argument-based approach** to validity, and
  name the threats it adds to each inference;
* audit an automated scorer with `ai_audit()`: Agreement with human raters,
  **differential scoring** across groups, **drift** across administrations
  and DIF on the test as scored;
* fold the results of difficulty models and item generators into the same
  audit;
* draft a validity argument with `validity_argument()`, and say what
  evidence no statistic can provide: Human oversight, disclosure and
  appeals.
</div>

**Key terms:**
[Validity argument](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#validity-argument),
[differential scoring](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#differential-scoring),
[DIF](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#dif),
[human-in-the-loop](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#human-in-the-loop),
[automated scoring](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#automated-scoring).

## The ideas

The earlier chapters of this part each checked one AI component on its own
terms: A scoring engine against human raters (Chapter
\@ref(auto-scoring)), a difficulty model by cross-validation (Chapter
\@ref(item-text)), an item generator by calibrating its families (Chapter
\@ref(aig)). A testing program needs one more step: To ask what the
components do to the **validity** of the scores, for the use the scores are
put to. The *Standards* [@aera2014] apply to AI components as to any other
part of a test, and the guidelines of the International Test Commission and
the Association of Test Publishers for technology-based assessment
[@itc2022] add advice on automated scoring, security and accessibility.

The **argument-based approach** [@kane2013] organizes the evidence. An
interpretation-and-use argument is a chain of inferences from a response to
a decision, each resting on a claim that evidence must support:

* **Scoring:** The score follows the rubric as trained raters apply it.
* **Generalization:** The score would be about the same with another
  occasion, form, rater or engine version.
* **Extrapolation:** The score reflects the construct, equally for all
  groups of test takers.
* **Decision:** Using the score for its purpose is appropriate.

An AI component adds threats to every link. A scoring engine may reward
features that are not in the rubric, such as length or vocabulary
[@williamson2012]. It may be retrained or updated by a vendor between
administrations, so that a score means something different from one year to
the next. It may treat groups differently: Answers that people would score
the same may get lower machine scores when they are typed on a phone or
written by English language learners. Johnson, Liu and McCaffrey
[-@johnson2022] separate two questions here. **Measurement bias** asks
whether the scores measure the construct equally for all groups, which is
the familiar DIF question. **Algorithmic bias** asks whether the engine
predicts the human score equally well for all groups, given the human
score. The second is checked by comparing machine and human scores within
groups among responses that people scored the same; we call a failure of
that check **differential scoring**.

The decision inference is different in kind. It is supported by how the
scores are used: Which responses a person reads before a score counts
(**human-in-the-loop**), what test takers are told about automated scoring,
how a score can be appealed, and how the component is monitored after it
goes live. These are matters of policy and documentation. An audit can show
which responses need a person; it cannot show that a person reads them.

## Example 1: Auditing a scoring engine

A college uses an automated engine to score two writing prompts, W1 and W2,
on a 0 to 4 rubric, for placement into first-year writing courses. Test
takers write in a spring or a fall window, on a laptop or a phone. A
validity sample of 30% is also scored by a person, and half of those by a
second person. We simulate the scores. The engine rewards length, and
answers typed on a phone are shorter, so on W2 it gives some phone answers
a point less than their true score. A stricter engine version was installed
for the fall window, and it marks down some W1 answers.

```{r data-ai-validity-1}
# Simulated machine and human scores of two writing prompts, 2,400 test takers.
set.seed(1818)
n <- 2400
writing <- data.frame(
  person = rep(sprintf("P%04d", 1:n), each = 2),
  window = rep(rep(c("Spring", "Fall"), each = n / 2), each = 2),
  device = rep(ifelse(runif(n) < 0.3, "Phone", "Laptop"), each = 2),
  prompt = rep(c("W1", "W2"), n))
theta <- rep(rnorm(n), each = 2)
true <- pmin(pmax(round(2 + 1.1 * theta + rnorm(2 * n, 0, 0.5)), 0), 4)
noisy <- function(x, p)        # off by one point with probability p
  pmin(pmax(x + ifelse(runif(length(x)) < p, sample(c(-1, 1), length(x), TRUE), 0), 0), 4)
writing$machine <- noisy(true, 0.25)
short <- writing$device == "Phone" & writing$prompt == "W2" & true > 1 & runif(2 * n) < 0.35
writing$machine[short] <- true[short] - 1          # shorter answers marked down
strict <- writing$window == "Fall" & writing$prompt == "W1" & true > 0 & runif(2 * n) < 0.30
writing$machine[strict] <- true[strict] - 1        # the fall engine version
read <- rep(runif(n) < 0.3, each = 2)
twice <- read & rep(runif(n) < 0.5, each = 2)
writing$human1 <- ifelse(read, noisy(true, 0.25), NA)
writing$human2 <- ifelse(twice, noisy(true, 0.25), NA)
writing$device <- factor(writing$device, levels = c("Laptop", "Phone"))
writing$window <- factor(writing$window, levels = c("Spring", "Fall"))
```

The usual first check is agreement with human raters, which
`agreement_report()` gives (Chapter \@ref(auto-scoring)):

```{r}
r <- writing[!is.na(writing$human1), ]
agreement_report(r$machine, r$human1, r$human2, by = r$prompt)
```

Both prompts meet the rules. `ai_audit()` runs this check and the others in
one call. The first group of `device` (Laptop) is the reference group, and
the first `window` (Spring) is the baseline for drift:

```{r}
audit <- ai_audit(writing, human2 = "human2", group = "device", item = "prompt",
                  period = "window")
audit
```

Agreement passes overall and within groups, but two checks block. The
differential scoring check compares the machine-minus-human difference of
phone and laptop answers that people scored the same:

```{r}
audit$differential
```

On W2, the engine scores phone answers about 0.2 SD lower than laptop
answers that people scored the same, four to five standard errors from
zero. This is what agreement within groups can miss: Phone users may also
score lower in truth (here they do not), so a lower mean alone proves
nothing, while a gap at the same human score is the engine's. The drift
check compares each window with the first:

```{r}
audit$drift[, c("item", "period", "n", "smd", "qwk", "smd_change", "p_change", "drift")]
```

In the fall, W1's machine scores fell to 0.2 SD below the human scores, and
agreement dropped. A drift flag needs both a change larger than the rule
and a change beyond sampling error; `p_change` is Bonferroni-adjusted across
the items and windows tested. Figure \@ref(fig:ai-validity-audit) shows the
three score checks.

```{r ai-validity-audit, fig.height = 3.4, fig.cap = "The score checks of the audit. Dashed lines are the limits of mv_rules(); bars are 95% confidence intervals."}
autoplot(audit)
```

When the test as scored is available, `responses` adds a DIF analysis with
`dif()`. DIF on an AI-scored item is flagged for review; DIF on an item the
engine does not score is reported for information, because it belongs to
content review, not to the engine. Lab 10 does this.

## Example 2: Other AI components

The same audit takes the results of the tools of the earlier chapters.
Here a difficulty model was trained with the proportion correct of the
field test among its features, and one of three item families is not
isomorphic:

```{r data-ai-validity-2}
# Simulated field-test results of 45 items from three item models.
set.seed(181)
fam <- rep(c("Ratios", "Fractions", "Equations"), each = 15)
b <- c(Ratios = -0.8, Fractions = 0, Equations = 0.9)[fam] +
  rnorm(45, 0, rep(c(0.1, 0.1, 0.5), each = 15))
items <- data.frame(id = sprintf("I%02d", 1:45), family = fam, b = b, b_se = 0.08,
                    words = round(25 + 5 * b + rnorm(45, 0, 6)),
                    p_field = round(plogis(-1.2 * b + rnorm(45, 0, 0.05)), 3))
```

```{r}
model <- predict_difficulty(items, c("family", "words", "p_field"), se = "b_se",
                            methods = "lltm")
families <- calibrate_families(items, family = "family", se = "b_se")
ai_audit(components = list(model, families))
```

The leaked feature blocks: Its predictions would vanish for new items that
have no field test (Chapter \@ref(item-text)). The family that is not
isomorphic is flagged for review: Its mean is a poor stand-in for new
items' difficulties (Chapter \@ref(aig)).

## Example 3: From audit to argument

`validity_argument()` turns the audit into a draft argument. Each inference
gets its claim, the threats an AI component adds, the evidence from the
audit and a status:

```{r}
va <- validity_argument(audit, construct = "academic writing in English",
                        use = "placement into first-year writing courses",
                        population = "incoming students")
va[, c("inference", "status")]
```

```{r}
cat(format(va, "markdown"))
```

The scoring inference is supported: The engine agrees with people as well
as they agree with each other. Generalization and extrapolation are
threatened by the fall engine version and by the phone gap. The decision
inference **needs evidence** whatever the audit finds, and the draft says
what: Human review of flagged responses (here, W2 answers typed on a phone,
and all fall W1 answers until the engine is fixed), disclosure to test
takers that their writing is scored by a machine, and a way to appeal.

The argument can go into the HTML report of the calibrated test with
`mv_report()`, as one more section:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
mv_report(fit, file = "writing-report.html",
          extra = list("Validity argument" = va))
```

## Governance

An audit at launch is not enough. A testing program that uses AI
components should also decide, and write down, the following. The
*Standards* [@aera2014] and the ITC/ATP guidelines [@itc2022] ask for
most of it in general terms.

* **Ownership.** Who is accountable for each component, including one
  bought from a vendor, and who may change it.
* **Change control.** Every new engine version, prompt or training set is
  audited on a validity sample before it goes live, as Example 1 shows why.
* **Human oversight.** Which responses a person reads: A share chosen at
  random for monitoring, every response the engine is unsure about, and
  any group or item where the audit found a problem until it is fixed.
* **Disclosure and appeals.** Test takers and score users are told how
  scores were produced, and a score can be rescored by a person on
  request.
* **Monitoring.** The audit is rerun on each administration, with its
  results in the technical report.
* **Data.** What test-taker data a component sees, where it is processed,
  and how long it is kept, especially when a language model runs on a
  provider's servers (Chapter \@ref(llms)).

Guidance on AI in testing is moving quickly. The checks in this chapter
rest on long-standing psychometric principles, but the regulations and
professional guidelines that apply should be checked at the time of use.

## Your turn

<div class="yourturn">
1. Rerun the audit of Example 1 with `mv_rules(subgroup_smd = 0.25)`.
   Which flags disappear, and what would the college then miss?
2. Audit only the spring window. Which problems does the audit find, and
   why is the fall engine version invisible?
3. Suppose the validity sample had included no phone answers to W2: Set
   their human scores to `NA` and rerun the audit. Does the differential
   scoring flag go away? What does that say about how the validity sample
   should be drawn?
4. Write the decision row of the validity argument for this college in
   your own words: Which responses would people read, what would the
   college tell students, and how would a student appeal?
</div>

<details><summary>Solutions</summary>

```{r}
# 1. a looser rule
ai_audit(writing, human2 = "human2", group = "device", item = "prompt",
         period = "window", rules = mv_rules(subgroup_smd = 0.25))$checks

# 2. the spring window alone
ai_audit(writing[writing$window == "Spring", ], human2 = "human2", group = "device",
         item = "prompt")$checks

# 3. without the phone answers to W2 in the validity sample
w3 <- writing
drop <- w3$device == "Phone" & w3$prompt == "W2"
w3$human1[drop] <- NA
w3$human2[drop] <- NA
ai_audit(w3, human2 = "human2", group = "device", item = "prompt")$differential
```

1. Both flags disappear: The phone gap (0.19 SD) and the fall drift (0.16
   SD) are below 0.25. The college would place phone users lower than
   their writing warrants on W2, and every fall W1 test taker lower than a
   spring one with the same answer. A rule should be set from the size of
   a difference that matters for placement, before the data are seen.
2. The phone gap on W2 is found (in a smaller sample, so with a wider
   interval); drift cannot be checked, because there is only one window.
   An audit can only find problems its data can show: Version changes need
   data from before and after.
3. The flag goes away, but not because the engine is fair: W2 has no
   phone answers with human scores left (`n` is 0), so there is no gap to
   compute, and the audit cannot flag what it cannot test. Its `checks`
   table shows one prompt tested instead of two. A validity sample must include every group and item the scores
   will be used for, in numbers large enough to detect a gap that matters.
4. For example: People read every W2 answer typed on a phone and every fall
   W1 answer until the engine is fixed, plus a random 10% of all answers
   and every answer near a placement cut. The placement letter says that
   writing is scored by an automated engine checked against trained
   raters, and that a student may ask for a human rescore within two weeks
   at no cost; the rescore replaces the machine score.

</details>

<div class="lab">
Lab 10, `run_lab("ai-audit")`, audits an AI-scored science test over two
years before its scores are released: Agreement, fairness to English
language learners, drift after an engine update, DIF on the test as scored,
and a validity argument for the committee. The [AI
Hub](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/ai-hub.html) collects
the other AI tools in mirtverse.
</div>

## Further reading {-}

Kane [-@kane2013] sets out the argument-based approach, and the
*Standards* [@aera2014] the evidence a testing program owes. Williamson,
Xi and Breyer [-@williamson2012] give the framework for evaluating
automated scoring that the agreement rules of mirtverse follow, and
Johnson, Liu and McCaffrey [-@johnson2022] show how to tell measurement
bias from algorithmic bias with tools a psychometrician already knows. The
ITC/ATP guidelines [-@itc2022] cover technology-based assessment more
broadly.
